info.bio:
Pulp es un grupo nacido en Sheffield, en Inglaterra a finales de los 70, aunque su primer disco se editó en 1983. Del grupo se destaca su carismático líder, Jarvis Cocker, uno de los estandartes del BritPop. La destreza a la hora de componer letras de Cocker fue creciendo y obtuvo su mayor reconocimiento en la mitad de los 90 con discos redondos como "His'n'Hers" o "Different Class".

podcast.title: Early Formation and Struggles (1981-1992)
podcast.body: Pulp formed very young, around ages 15-16, in Sheffield, at roughly the same time as bands like Joy Division and Siouxsie and the Banshees, predating even New Order. Despite their early start, they struggled for approximately 15 years to achieve success, spending over a decade experimenting with various styles like New Wave, synthesizers, and Post-Punk, and releasing early albums on small, ineffective labels with poor or no critical reception. "Palt is a very curious group because although it was one of the pillars of Brit-Pop Palt was forming almost at the same time as groups like Joy Division or like Suixion de Bansis then."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: 1996 Mercury Music Prize Winner
podcast.body: Pulp achieved significant recognition by winning the 1996 Mercury Music Prize, an award that highlights the best British albums of the year. Their album was released in the fall of 1995, during Britpop's momentum. "Pulp from the fall of 1995 and the winner of the 1996 Mercury Music Prize."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Crashing Michael Jackson's Brit Awards Performance (1996)
podcast.body: On February 19, 1996, Jarvis Cocker of Pulp walked onto the stage during Michael Jackson's "Earth Song" performance at the Brit Awards, where Jackson was surrounded by children, and shook his bum at the audience as a protest against Jackson's self-perception as a "Christ-like figure with the power of healing." Cocker was arrested but not charged, and was widely hailed for speaking what "everyone was thinking." "It was a form of protest that the way Michael Jackson sees himself as some Christ-like figure with the power of healing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2

podcast.title: Trainspotting Soundtrack Contribution (1996)
podcast.body: Pulp contributed to the first *Trainspotting* soundtrack in 1996. This soundtrack gained widespread acclaim and is often listed among the best movie soundtracks of all time, known for its mix of old and new rock and electronic music that captured the film's desperate yet uplifting tone. "New Order, Pulp, Blur, Underworld, Elastica, Lou Reed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jarvis Cocker's Cocaine Addiction (1997)
podcast.body: In 1997, Jarvis Cocker struggled with a severe cocaine addiction, which significantly impacted the band's performances and creative output. Recordings from their concerts that year show some to be "truly pathetic," with anecdotes like Jarvis Cocker vomiting on stage in Spain. This addiction also contributed to a creative block, where he struggled to write new material after "Different Class." "a serious problem was the addition to cocaine by Jarvis Cocker that caused during a year, well, there are recordings of the concerts in 1997 of Palt that some are truly pathetic."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Steve Mackey Death (March 2, 2023) – Undisclosed Illness, Age 56; Produced Florence and the Machine's Lungs; Appeared in Harry Potter
podcast.body: Steve Mackey joined Pulp in 1989 and was their bassist through the glory years of the 1990s Britpop era before leaving around 2002. He became a producer and remix artist, working with Cornershop, The Kills, and The Horrors, and co-produced Florence and the Machine's debut album *Lungs*. He also worked as a music director and sound designer for institutions including the Louvre, the Museum of Modern Art, and a Shanghai museum. Harry Potter fans may know him as one of the Weird Sisters in *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire* — a group that also featured Jarvis Cocker of Pulp and Johnny Greenwood and Phil Selway of Radiohead. When Pulp announced a reunion in early 2023, Mackey did not want to participate — in retrospect, probably because he was already ill. His death was announced March 2, 2023, having been in hospital since Christmas 2022 with an undisclosed condition. He was 56. "In retrospect, that's probably because he was ill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artsy Style and Observational Lyrics
podcast.body: Pulp was noted for being "more artsy than most," with lead singer Jarvis Cocker's lyrics frequently characterized as "observational." This lyrical approach was a key influence on the Arctic Monkeys.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artwork Designer
podcast.body: Peter Saville, chief art design guy at Factory Records, did design work for Pulp. "He did everything from gig posters to album design for Joy Division New Order, Roxas music, Swade, pulp, Martha Nemuffins, and Noam D."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Britpop Peak
podcast.body: Pulp reached its Britpop peak with Russell Senior as a guitarist and violinist, though singer Jarvis Cocker (referred to as "Jarvis Pulp" in the transcript) was noted to be getting most of the attention during this period. "He was with them at their Brit Pot Peak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contemporary Glam Trappings
podcast.body: Pulp is listed as an act exhibiting "Glam trappings" in their music and visual style, demonstrating glam's ongoing influence in later decades. "and Pulp."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Departure from Britpop
podcast.body: Pulp easily abandoned Britpop, having previously experimented with various stylistic shifts. This allowed them to pursue a completely independent path shortly after the movement's decline. "Pulp que había dado varios tumbos estilísticos, había probado de todo, había hecho de todo pues tampoco le costó demasiado abandonar el ripop"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Fans Dancing to Electronic Music
podcast.body: Pulp fans were seen dancing to The Chemical Brothers' music at rock festivals, a novel sight in the early 1990s that demonstrated the Big Beat movement's ability to bridge electronic and rock cultures. "gente que escuchaba o así o que escuchaba a Blur o que escuchaba a PULP y que de repente estaban bayando a los chemical brothers."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: The Chemical Brothers. Padres de la cultura BIG BEAT

podcast.title: Founding and Obscurity
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker founded Pulp in Sheffield in 1978. The band "languished in obscurity for a decade and a half," not even registering as a footnote in British music before their breakthrough in the mid-1990s. "Jarvis Cocker founded Pulp in Sheffield in 1978."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indefinite Hiatus
podcast.body: Pulp went on an indefinite hiatus after the Britpop era came to an end. "Pulp went on an indefinite hiatus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jarvis Cocker's Charismatic Persona
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker was a uniquely British figure, embodying an "old school" Britishness with an eccentric and strange yet highly charismatic and attractive personality. His interviews from 1993-94 showed him to be engaging and humorous, contributing significantly to Pulp's appeal. "Jarvis Cocker was a character, there are few people more British than Jarvis Cocker."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Jarvis Cocker's Dream of Stardom
podcast.body: The entire history of Pulp is deeply intertwined with Jarvis Cocker's personal quest to become a major star, driven not primarily by exceptional musical talent or ambition, but by a profound desire for superstardom against significant odds. This ambition defined Pulp's early, often difficult, years. "all the history of the band is summarized in the personal history of Jarvis Cocker fighting to pursue a dream that is to be a great star."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Jarvis Cocker's Iconic Voice
podcast.body: While Jarvis Cocker's vocal style received mixed and sometimes "terribly bad" criticism upon the release of "His 'n' Hers," particularly from a significant portion of critics who were "horrified" by his singing, his voice eventually became an iconic and distinctive element of 90s UK music. "the way Jarvis Cocker sings is already an icon of the 90s in the United Kingdom."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Late Entry and Prior Struggles
podcast.body: Pulp's entry into the Britpop generation was unique, as they had been active for over 10 years, released several albums, and had little success while moving between various independent labels before joining the movement. "Pulp llega a la generación del Brit-Pulp cuando llevaba más de 10 años en el mercado. Había sacado varios discos, no había tenido mucho éxito, había pululado por varias discográficas independientes."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Long History and Mid-90s Success
podcast.body: Pulp had been active since the late 1970s but did not achieve significant success until the mid-1990s, coinciding with when the Arctic Monkeys were in junior high. This timing meant Pulp was an unavoidable presence for young, aspiring musicians in Sheffield.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Long Obscurity Before Britpop Success
podcast.body: Pulp, founded by Jarvis Cocker in 1978, "languished in obscurity for a decade and a half," barely registering in British music history until their 1994 album *His 'n' Hers* and especially their 1995 album *Different Class*. "Jarvis Cocker founded Pulp in 1978. They'd languished in obscurity for a decade and a half."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Long Road to Success
podcast.body: Pulp's journey to success was notably protracted, spanning nearly 15 years and marked by numerous stylistic shifts ("tumbos") before they finally achieved prominence. This extended period of development stood in stark contrast to the rapid rise of bands like Oasis. "Palp estuvo casi 15 años dando tumbos en lado a otro hasta que tuvo el cito."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Polygram and Island Records' Bet
podcast.body: Polygram and Island Records eventually backed Pulp almost "by elimination" because the band was relatively "burnt out" in the music market. To ensure success for a band with a decade of minimal success, the labels decided to invest heavily financially. "Island Records y Polygram acabaron apostando por Pulp casi un poco por eliminación, porque al final era una banda ya relativamente quemada en el mercado musical."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Post-Brit-Pop Evolution
podcast.body: Pulp, unlike some of their Brit-Pop contemporaries, successfully transitioned out of the genre, refusing to be confined by a dying movement. Their long history of stylistic experimentation prepared them for this shift, leading to a new musical direction for Jarvis Cocker inspired by Scott Walker. "Palp was one of those bands that managed to escape Brit-Pop quite quickly and not look back and not get stuck in a dying movement."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Post-Britpop Diversification
podcast.body: As the Britpop movement faded, Pulp actively diversified its sound, moving into new genres. Examples mentioned include "doing hardcore" and "doing a lofi album," illustrating the band's efforts to escape the confines of the Britpop genre and explore new musical territories. "el palp estaba haciendo DCs hardcore, estaba haciendo un disco de lofi."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Post-Britpop Hiatus
podcast.body: Pulp "went on an indefinite hiatus" after the Britpop era concluded, putting their activities on hold without a defined return. "and pulp went on an indefinite hiatus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Pulp's Brit-Pop Identity
podcast.body: Within the Brit-Pop movement, Pulp carved out a distinct niche, representing a more "kitsch" sensibility, sometimes drawing comparisons to acts like The B-52s or bizarre New Wave. This unique stylistic path allowed them to stand apart from other bands like Blur (more agile, fun) or Oasis (more classic British rock). "if Blur was that more agile, more movement, more agile, more fun British, and Oasis was that more classic British movement of Paul Weller and the Rolling Stones, if The Jam, then Pulp was that more kitsch movement, which sometimes reminded of The B-52s, sometimes reminded of that somewhat bizarre New Wave."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Reunion for Touring
podcast.body: Pulp was one of many bands from past decades that reunited in the 21st century, a trend largely motivated by financial incentives. With declining CD sales impacting artist revenues, returning to the touring circuit offered a lucrative way to appeal to nostalgic fan bases and fill large venues. "The list of reunions is long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: The Truth and Beauty, The True Story of Pulp
podcast.body: This 700-page book is considered the only reliable and accurate biography of Pulp. Unlike many bands, Pulp does not have an official biography, largely due to Jarvis Cocker's deliberate effort to not recall or provide much information about the band's first ten to twelve years. This book is the primary source for all serious articles and documentation about the band. "the only correct biography we have of Palt which has 700 pages which is called The Truth and Beauty, The Truth Story of Palt."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Unavoidable Influence in Sheffield
podcast.body: For anyone growing up in Sheffield, England, during the mid-90s, Pulp was an inescapable part of the musical landscape, making them a strong influence on local bands like the Arctic Monkeys.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unusual Entry into Britpop
podcast.body: Among the four main pillars of Britpop, Pulp stood out as a peculiar case because they were a much older band than the others, despite being identified as a defining act of the movement. Their long history before the Britpop era made their entry unique.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
